title: Metal Fabrication Invoice Template
subtitle: An invoice pre-filled for metal fabrication shops — shop hours, CAD design time, steel stock with markup, CNC plasma cutting, press-brake bends, machining, and delivery. Download as Excel (auto-calculating), Word, or PDF.
taxHint: Look up your state's sales tax rate
paymentTerms: 50% deposit before material purchase; balance due on pickup or delivery. Repeat commercial accounts: Net 30 with approved credit.
notes: Thank you for your business. Dimensions, material grade, and tolerances per approved drawing. Tolerances ±1/16 in. unless noted. Repeat runs skip design fees — ask about second-run pricing.

features: Auto-calculating tax formulas in Excel — just enter your state rate
Pre-filled fab-shop line items — shop hours, design time, steel with markup, plasma cuts, bends, machining
Material listed with its markup as its own line — customers see steel cost and shop labor separately
Deposit terms built in — 50% up front covers steel before you ever cut it

faqs.q: What should I include on a metal fabrication invoice?
faqs.a: Your business details, the client, and a job or drawing number that ties the invoice to the approved prints. Break the work into its real steps: shop hours, design time, material with its grade (A36, 304 stainless, 5052 aluminum) and thickness, plasma or laser cutting by the part, bends by the bend, machining by the hole, finishing, and delivery. Note tolerances and finish spec in the notes, then tax and total.

faqs.q: How much does metal fabrication cost?
faqs.a: Shop labor runs $60–$120 per hour depending on region and process (design/CAD $75–$125/hr, welding $75–$125/hr). Steel passes through at cost plus 20–30% handling. CNC cutting bills $4–$10 per part plus setup, press-brake work $5–$15 per bend, and drilled or tapped features $2–$5 each. Typical jobs: a custom trailer gate $250–$600, welded handrails $65–$125 per linear foot, a small production run of brackets $8–$20 each.

faqs.q: Should I mark up material on the invoice?
faqs.a: Yes — 20–30% on steel stock is the industry norm, and it should be its own line. The markup covers sourcing, handling, cut-off scrap, and the risk of steel price moves between quote and build. List the material as 'cost + 25% handling' so the customer understands the number; shops that bury material inside an hourly rate end up eating price spikes.

faqs.q: Why take a deposit on fabrication work?
faqs.a: Because the steel gets bought before the first cut. A 50% deposit on material and setup protects you when a customer changes their mind mid-build — metal cut to a drawing has almost no resale value. Collect the deposit against a written quote or work order, then invoice the balance on pickup or delivery.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate tax automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, tax and total update automatically. Leave the tax rate blank if fabrication services are not taxable in your state.

deepDive.heading: Fabrication shop invoicing: per-piece, per-hour and stock-material billing
deepDive.sub: A fabrication job mixes engineering time, machine time and material bought at mill prices. Billing it as "fabrication — $4,200" hides where the money went and makes every change order a fight. Here is how shops itemize it.

blocks.h3: Three clocks run at once: programming, machine time and bench time
paras: A laser or plasma cut part is charged three ways and conflating them is the usual estimating error. Programming and nesting is a one-off cost per drawing — half an hour to two hours for a simple bracket, more if the drawing needs cleanup before it can be cut. Machine time is billed at an hourly rate that should already carry the consumables, the power and the depreciation on a machine that costs six figures. Bench time is fit-up, deburring, drilling, tapping and inspection, and it is the part every shop underestimates.

On the invoice, split the three so the customer sees the logic. "Cutting — 0.4 hr @ $145/hr" tells them the job was small; "fabrication — $58" tells them nothing. When they come back with a drawing revision, you can then quote the reprogramming as a line rather than absorbing it.
list: Programming/nesting: quoted as a setup charge, not hourly — usually $75-200 per new drawing
Machine time: laser/plasma $120-200/hr, press brake $85-150/hr, machining $90-180/hr
Bench/fit-up: 25-40% of total labour on most fabrication work
Finish: deburr included, powder coat and paint priced per square foot or per part

blocks.h3: Stock material is billed at mill price plus a cut and handling margin
paras: Material is the line customers audit hardest. A fabrication shop does not buy small quantities at mill prices — it buys drops and remnants from a service centre, or cuts from its own stock bought months ago at a different price. Billing at today's mill price plus 15-25% for handling is standard practice and defensible if the invoice states the grade, the thickness and the size.

List plate and sheet as thickness x width x length, and structural shapes by designation — A36 angle 2x2x1/4, A992 wide flange W8x10, 304 stainless sheet. If the customer supplied the material, say so explicitly with a zero-value line: a supplied-material job with no note looks like a billing error when the total is half the quote.
list: Grade and thickness on every material line: A36, A572-50, A992, 304/316 stainless, 6061 aluminium
Remnant/drop stock priced at current replacement cost, not historic cost
Cut charge separate from stock price — cutting is labour, stock is material
Customer-supplied material: zero-value line plus a note that handling is still billable

blocks.h3: Prototype, one-off and production runs price differently
paras: A prototype is engineering work with an unknown outcome: the customer pays for the attempt, not for a guaranteed part, and the invoice should say so. One-off parts carry the full setup cost across a single unit. Production runs spread setup across the batch, so the per-piece price falls sharply — a bracket at $85 each for one piece might be $22 each at a hundred, and the invoice should show the setup line amortized rather than hiding it.

When a customer asks for "a hundred of these" after buying one at prototype pricing, the correct move is a new quote with the setup broken out, not the prototype rate multiplied by a hundred. Put the pricing basis on the invoice: "one-off rate" and "production rate (setup included, 100 pcs)" are two different documents.
list: Prototype: time and materials, no fixed-price guarantee, revision billed as new work
One-off: full setup and programming charged to the single piece
Production: setup amortized across the batch, per-piece rate stated with the quantity
Tooling and fixtures built for the job remain your property unless sold separately

blocks.h3: Tolerances, inspection and certification are billable scope
paras: A drawing with a general tolerance block is not the same as a drawing with a critical ±0.005 in feature, and they do not cost the same to make. Tight tolerances need better machines, slower feeds, more frequent checks and often a CMM report. If the customer's drawing carries a tolerance you did not price, you have agreed to it for free.

Inspection paperwork is a line item in regulated industries: material test reports (MTRs) for structural work, first-article inspection reports, dimensional reports, and certificates of conformance. Shops give these away and then resent the two hours it takes to produce them. Bill them, or at minimum state that they are included so the customer knows they received something of value.
list: Tolerance class on the quote: general (ISO 2768-m) vs critical features called out individually
MTRs for structural steel — required on load-bearing work, billable as documentation
First-article inspection (FAI) report for production runs
Certificate of conformance: a one-page document, but it is the customer's audit trail

blocks.h3: The invoice terms that keep a shop out of trouble
paras: Fabrication shops live on deposits and progress payments because material is bought before the job is paid. Fifty percent on order is normal for a first-time customer, and material-heavy jobs often go thirty percent on order, forty on delivery of the cut parts, thirty on completion. Net 30 is for established accounts only.

Two clauses do most of the work on a fabrication invoice: the quote validity (steel moves weekly, so 15 or 30 days) and the delivery/risk clause (who owns the parts in transit, who pays the freight, when title passes). Add a restocking or cancellation charge for custom-cut material — once a plate is cut to size it cannot go back into stock.
list: Deposit: 50% on order for new customers, progress billing on long jobs
Quote validity 15-30 days with a steel escalation clause beyond that
Freight: FOB shop or delivered — state which, and who insures transit
Custom-cut material non-cancellable once cutting begins
